ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The circuit shows an op-amp. The input voltage ui is connected through resistor R1 to the inverting '-' input. The non-inverting '+' input is connected to ground through resistor R2. Resistor Rf is drawn as a feedback resistor from the output node uo back to the inverting input node. Reasoning: If Rf becomes unsoldered, the feedback path is removed and the op-amp works open-loop. For an ideal op-amp, the input current is approximately zero, so no current flows through R1 and the inverting input voltage is v- = ui. Since ui < 0, v- < 0. The non-inverting input is grounded through R2, so v+ = 0. Therefore v+ - v- > 0, so the op-amp output saturates positively. Thus uo = +Uom.

method.method_draft: First describe the circuit in the image: ui reaches the '-' input through R1, the '+' input is grounded through R2, and Rf would be feedback from uo to the '-' node. Since Rf is unsoldered, remove the feedback path. With ideal op-amp input current nearly zero, the '-' input voltage equals ui, so v- = ui < 0; the '+' input voltage is grounded, so v+ = 0. Thus v+ - v- > 0, so the open-loop op-amp drives to its positive saturation. Therefore uo = +Uom.

method.method_draft: Begin by noting from the image that the normal closed-loop inverting amplifier depends on Rf connecting uo back to the '-' input. If Rf becomes unsoldered, that negative-feedback loop is broken, so do not use the inverting amplifier gain formula. Instead, compare the two op-amp input terminals: the '+' terminal is tied to ground through R2, while the '-' terminal is driven through R1 by the given negative input ui. Since ui < 0, the inverting terminal is below ground and the non-inverting terminal is higher. Hence the op-amp output goes to the positive saturation limit, uo = Uom.
